articleTitle: ALINEA: a local feedback control law for on-ramp metering; a real-life study
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: A detailed investigation of the performance and effectiveness of strategies for motorway congestion reduction involving metering and control on motorway access ramps showed that significant improvements in traffic conditions have been obtained. This improvement is a function of the strategy tested. The best tested control strategy was found to be ALINEA, which was developed on the basis of classical control theory methods and which was the only strategy using feedback in a systematic way. Compared to beaconing, ALINEA leads to an increase of 3% with respect to the number of vehicles served, a decrease of 55% with respect to the time spent in congestion, and a decrease of 19% with respect to the mean travel time. ALINEA also proved superior in terms of the time during which the control override was active. Furthermore, this strategy diverts fewer vehicles than the other tested strategies. In fact, ALINEA was found to be a simple, efficient strategy which could be generalized in a coordinated ramp control scheme including the whole Boulevard Peripherique of Paris.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An algorithm for prediction of travel time using vehicle sensor data
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Travel time is usually calculated by dividing a route into several subsections and totaling travel time measured by vehicle sensors in each subsection. The disadvantage of this method is that the vehicle length is always assumed to be constant despite changes in traffic conditions. The paper proposes a new approach which introduces a time series model and a statistical presumption of vehicle length. Using the former, one can predict changes in traffic conditions from origin to destination during the passage of time. With the latter, one can calculate travel time from the point of origin. To evaluate the validity of the approach, the author conducted an experiment on national road Route 16, in Chiba Prefecture, Japan.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Drivers' requirements for route guidance
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Following a series of group discussions and in depth interviews, a questionnaire was developed which sought to establish the sorts of route guidance and advice that users might require in different circumstances. The questionnaire was designed such that the respondents would complete it at home and return it by post. Distribution was to be by hand to peoples' homes with a brief verbal description by survey staff of the purpose of the survey. Two thousand copies were distributed in London during July 1989 and a 40% response rate was achieved. The questionnaire was translated, as closely as possible, into German and French. In the paper the authors analyse the results of the questionnaire.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Travel times as a basic part of the LISB guidance strategy
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The Berlin LISB Guidance and Information system is an individual, dynamic guidance system for motorised vehicles. LISB works in accordance with the principle of central route searching. Within a cycle of a few minutes, a computer in the traffic control centre of the road transport authorities calculates and offers the quickest routes for any given O-D relation in the entire urban area. The vehicle transmits to the beacon the travel and queueing times which it has gained from the network since it passed the last beacon; it then receives information about the quickest route to all surrounding beacons as well as the allocation of these routes to the destination coordinates. Thus, the navigation device can select the links by which the vehicle finds its destination. Over the day, travel times vary with the traffic volumes on the links of the network. Therefore a recommendation of quickest routes must not be static. The authors consider the role of travel time prediction and the methods for measuring times for the guidance system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Recent enhancements to SCOOT-SCOOT Version 2.4
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The SCOOT (Split Cycle Offset Optimisation Technique) vehicle-responsive traffic control signal system described by Hunt el al (1981) has been commercially available for over seven years and is now installed in over 40 cities in the UK and overseas. Projects had been carried out, which were aimed at making SCOOT more aware and be able to react to what was actually happening on street by providing feedback of signal status and by measuring the saturation flow rate online, and to provide additional facilities within SCOOT for dealing with severe congestion. These projects were completed in 1989 and the results of the work have been combined with other enhancements developed at TRRL to produce the latest release of SCOOT, Version 2.4. The paper describes the new features of Version 2.4.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MOVA control of isolated traffic signals-recent experience
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: MOVA is a control strategy using a new detector layout for isolated traffic signals (ie not co-ordinated with any other traffic signalled junctions). It is a self-optimising system designed to reduce delays and stops, and to maximise capacity during peak periods. The paper presents some of the results and experiences of the 20 site trial programme. The objective of the trial is to validate and verify the installation of MOVA add-on units into a variety of approved traffic signal controller types and junction layouts. The MOVA equipment has undergone an approval exercise with the Department of Transport, and will be approved for use as an add-on unit throughout Britain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An evaluation of microwave vehicle detection at traffic signal controlled intersections
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Reliable vehicle detectors are an essential element in traffic surveillance and control. The development of strategies for the improvement of safety and reduction of congestion at intersections often hinges on good quality vehicle detection. The paper concerns microwave vehicle detectors (MVDs). MVDs have been installed at many pelican crossings and temporary traffic signal controlled junctions due to their low cost and ease of installation and maintenance. The paper reports on an investigation, conducted in Edinburgh, into their operational performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Combining traffic management and driver information in integrated traffic networks
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: In response to a need to develop a model which could simultaneously represent signalized surface streets and freeways during congested traffic conditions, the INTEGRATION traffic simulation model was developed. The paper describes how various features have been implemented and what types of findings have been derived from tests using this model. In addition, the types of additional improvements that are expected to be needed to address the growing demands that are being placed on today's combined traffic control and route guidance simulation models are also discussed. The first part of this paper summarizes the overall design of the INTEGRATION model before it is indicated how various traffic signal and freeway control features are modelled within INTEGRATION. Subsequently, the specific features dealing with traffic congestion are introduced, before the route assignment and route guidance features of the model are presented. Finally, the current status of the model and its related support routines are discussed and further developments are prioritized.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A simulation tool for traffic signal control planning
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The testing and evaluation of alternative signal control strategies is time consuming and the classic methods in delay and queue length estimation do not always give sufficient and valid information in changing traffic conditions. New ways are therefore needed. One possible method is advanced computer simulation. To be useful in signal control planning and research a simulator must be able to simulate the functions of the signal controller; and the behaviour and reactions of traffic flow to the signals. The paper summarizes the principles and experiences gained so far in the building and testing of this new kind of a simulator at The Helsinki University of Technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Road traffic monitoring using image processing
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: A method is described which provides data on traffic congestion over a length of roadway using inexpensive image processing and computing hardware. It provides distinct advantages over more conventional methods since data is collected over a region rather than a point in the road network. Furthermore, the state of the network can be deduced within a time scale comparable to the period with which congestion occurs on a busy road after an incident has occurred. Action can be taken on information acquired directly from the scene and not inferred from statistics built up over a period of minutes. Further work is required to take account of minor perspective distortion effects, which can cause false alarms when single vehicles occupy the distant end of the window. A measure of the amount of traffic in the window will also be needed to enable comparison with other regions of the network. Night time scenes have not been included in the test program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of SCOOT in developing countries
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The SCOOT system of reducing delay to traffic in an urban traffic signal controlled network was developed by the Transport and Road Research Laboratory and British industry to maximise the capacity of existing roads in congested town centres. As a result SCOOT is very robust in accommodating great changes in the timing of traffic demand or flow pattern. It also enables traffic growth to be accommodated without any further action by the traffic engineer. This would seem to make SCOOT ideal for use in developing countries where traffic growth is at a high rate and skilled engineers are in great demand. The paper describes the application of an urban traffic control system with SCOOT in Beijing, the capital of the Peoples Republic of China.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Specific pedestrian crossing traffic lights
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: In 1982, the local authorities of the City of Toulouse began investigations to improve the safety of pedestrians, particularly on pedestrians crossings outside intersections. New solutions have then been developed concerning the control of these crossing by traffic lights, starting from existing equipments and rules. A specific equipment, better suited to the specific need of pedestrian protection on street crossing, has then been developed, in collaboration with the French Ministry of Transports (Direction de la Securite et de la Circulation Routiere). The equipment include: signals for drivers indicating pedestrian crossing, and the pedestrian lights with green-and red-main lights and an additional third yellow light.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PRODYN: on site evaluation
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper deals with the on-site evaluation of the PRODYN method. The idea of PRODYN was inspired by studies on the off-line computation of a short sample time optimal control of an intersection using backward dynamic programming. From that initial point, research has been conducted since 1978 it has consisted of: finding a suboptimal optimization method to compute the controls on-line; finding the best method for coordination of intersections controllers; developing a queue estimator; and improving the traffic model used. The simulation tests realized during this research showed the interest of the method, and on site experiments were conducted in 1987 on an isolated intersection and in 1988 on a 7 intersections network. The authors present the tested algorithm and describe the implementation of a PRODYN prototype on the system of the Zone Experimentale et Laboratoire de Trafic de Toulouse (ZELT). The authors also present the evaluation of the control strategy on the isolated intersection and the network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SCOOT : a traffic database
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The SCOOT traffic responsive urban traffic control system has been installed in over 30 towns and cities in the UK and overseas. The primary purpose of SCOOT is the optimisation of signal timings in a network according to current traffic conditions to reduce overall traffic delay. However, in the process of optimisation SCOOT's traffic model provides a wealth of traffic information which is potentially useful for a variety of purposes. The paper describes a study carried out by the Transportation Research Group (TRG) of Southampton University for the Transport and Road Research Laboratory (TRRL) into the development and production of a SCOOT traffic database, aimed at realising the potential of the data within SCOOT systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of a lorry monitoring and identification system
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: This paper describes a project to develop, install and commission a prototype system to monitor and photograph lorries contravening lorry bans. The prototype enforcement system described consists of two main components: a vehicle detection system incorporating piezo sensors; and a camera system which is used to photograph vehicles of interest. Tests of the system at a trial site in Welham Green, Hertfordshire, UK, have shown that it is effective in identifying heavy goods vehicles that are potential ban violators. This is the first time that a classification system has been successfully implemented which seeks to classify vehicles according to 'plated' gross vehicle weight. Based on the prototype installed and tested at Welham Green, the SHERIFF law enforcement system has been developed. This could play an important role in assisting police authorities in the monitoring and enforcement of traffic highway violations. This will be particularly true when laws are passed allowing prosecutions for speeding and red-light offences to be made on the basis of photographic evidence alone.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Data and route guidance
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Describes the data components of a dynamic route guidance system and addresses the issues of: complexity of the database; collection of real-time data from various sources; accuracy and quality of information; and by-products of data accumulated by such a system. The detail is based upon the authors' experience in supporting the London Autoguide Demonstrator Project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control and communications systems on major urban routes in the UK
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Some high speed roads have a special need for control and management. Since their introduction in the 1970s, control and communications systems have become a standard feature of all UK motorways. However, major roads which have been or are being upgraded for higher traffic speeds or improved traffic flows do not have control and communications facilities to a common standard such as is apparent on motorways. This paper considers two regions of road construction proposals: the East London Road Network and the North Circular Road; and the A55 North Wales Coast Road. Features considered for the systems are telephones, alarm push buttons in tunnels, matrix signal indicators, lane control signs, variable messages, loop detection, tunnel E&M monitoring, CCTV, tunnel entry prohibition signs, and radio communications in tunnels.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Road pricing in the Netherlands
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: One of the measures proposed in the Netherlands for safeguarding and improving traffic mobility in the densely populated areas is Rekening Rijden. Rekening Rijden (RR) is aimed at a reduction of traffic flow in the Netherlands in general and a specific reduction of traffic flow within the Randstad at peak hours by increasing the variable costs of car driving by extra charging the use of heavily used roads in this area at peak hours. The RR system is designed to meet European standards and is open to other applications such as user information systems, fleet management systems, and traffic guidance systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Introducing light rail transit into streets
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Continuing operation of LRT systems in Europe and elsewhere shows that LRT can alleviate congestion and is a practical proposition. The accidents relating to recent LRT introductions show that the phase where a new LRT is introduced into streets is a phase requiring special attention and planning. The LRT is to serve a community. If the community objects to it, it may delay its opening or impose operating constraints which reduce financial return. This paper raises the key issues requiring attention if the LRT is to be accepted, valued and trusted by its community. When managing the major project of introducing LRVs into streets, the preceding project phases must incorporate consideration of commissioning as an activity itself. This requires cooperation between engineering and operating functions for the LRT to achieve successful integration into road traffic on the streets of our towns and cities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TELESIC operation: urban grand boulevard management
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Concerns the control of traffic on the Grand Boulevard linking Lille, Roubaix and Tourcoing in France. First, where it is not a dual carriageway, a low wall was built in the middle of the road. Then, the TELESIC system was introduced. It has five functions: surveillance and traffic movement reporting in real time; provision of information on congestion; traffic light control, to ease congestion; incident detection; and speed checking.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Are we signalling safely (traffic control signals)
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: With ever increasing constraints on new road building, particularly within the urban environment, the efficient management of the existing road network is becoming more and more important. It could be argued that the most significant contribution to efficient road management has come from traffic signals. With the development of microprocessors and integrated circuits has come a whole range of new and increasingly sophisticated signalling techniques. The wide-spread adoption of these new techniques indicates a degree of consensus regarding their success at managing the road system efficiently, but what about their impact on safety. Clearly, safety and signals must be interlinked if only by means of geography. The paper looks at the implications of signals on safety and poses the question 'are we signalling safely?' In doing so, consideration is given to various signalling techniques and what is known about their safety benefits and disbenefits.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The effects of traffic management and control on vehicle capacity in London
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Journey speed is a good measure of the performance of a road system in a town, provided it allows journeys to be made by a reasonably direct route. Journey speed and its changes have also been used as a measure of performance of the effect of traffic management schemes. The standard method of measurement, a moving observer car technique, was used extensively in the measurement of the effects of urban traffic control techniques (UTC). It has been shown that journey time reductions of at least 12% could be achieved by UTC. However, introducing UTC and other traffic management techniques in London, has not increased the average journey speed as measured by the regular surveys. There is clearly a finite limit to the capacity of a road network during which traffic moves at an acceptable speed. Attempts have been made to predict this and a method by Wardrop (1976) is described. This shows that the traffic capacity of the network has increased over the years but recent data suggests that it has probably reached a maximum. The author considers whether the application of further traffic management techniques such as SCOOT and Autoguide will achieve the actual improvements that are predicted by theoretical techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ZELT: a European full-scale laboratory for urban traffic
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: In all countries which have to face urban traffic problems, the need of field trials for systems or strategies appears and field trials remain indispensable. The author describes the role of ZELT in answering the needs of field trials. ZELT is an urban test site which was built between 1982 and 1986 by the French Ministry of Transports with the help and cooperation of the City of Toulouse. It includes field equipment shared around 20 intersections and a central control room (PC ZELT) near the city center.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ASTER: a statistical tool for urban traffic data analysis
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The authors introduce a statistical traffic analysis for management and control software package, called ASTER, which can be implemented on microcomputers. The package features: dedicated to urban traffic data analysis; using advanced statistical methods, such as factorial analysis and automated clustering; can be used by non-statisticians; and presenting a wide range of visualisation and representation tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of detector data for traffic control strategies
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper begins by describing the role traffic detection systems play in enabling an expert system to define remedial control strategies for congestion management. It highlights the need for algorithms to infer the traffic conditions and route patterns in a city network and justifies the need to study the origin and destinations of all vehicles entering, leaving and travelling within subarea of a SCOOT system, whilst simultaneously monitoring traffic with SCOOT detectors. Finally, the design and results of a number plate survey is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vihdintie roundabout-new approach in high-performance signal control
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Vihdintie roundabout is a five-arm conventional roundabout with some 140 m in diameter. It is located in a western suburban area in Helsinki and it connects three important main roads together. A theoretical five-arm roundabout signalling model was studied with Transyt. Only the offsets and splits were optimised. A cycle time of 60 seconds was chosen because of analytical considerations. The size of the roundabout was chosen so that the travel time round the system was assumed to be 40 seconds. The study shows that the optimisation of timings with Transyt is very useful, especially the possibility of handling all traffic streams separately with the shared stopline-option. Traffic actuated control mode is suitable for roundabout signalling. Some special control logic should be used, which maintains the good progression of vehicles through adjacent stoplines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The American double ring system applied in London
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The junction of the A10 Great Cambridge Road and Bullsmoor Lane is the northern most signal installation in London. Consideration was given to solutions which would employ to the full, the benefits of microprocessor technology. One of the concepts considered was the double ring concept employed in American controllers and it was decided that with development it would be appropriate for the Great Cambridge Road and Bullsmoor Lane junction. Despite the difficulties associated with the specification it is considered that this method of control is a useful additional measure for engineers. It reduces the levels of lost time for phases in conflict with relatively light flows.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The organisation and operation of traffic control maintenance
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Improvements to the organisation and operation of traffic control maintenance can, obtain rates of return similar to those obtained by other more glamorous projects, and can play a significant role in the alleviation of congestion in towns and cities. In the present paper the organisation and operation of traffic control maintenance are described and discussed under the following headings: fault reporting, processing and inspection; organisation of maintenance and contract arrangements; effect of design and installation on maintenance; and legal considerations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Nottinghamshire's red light camera experiment
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Describes a system, tested in Nottinghamshire, UK, for the detection of road vehicles that pass red traffic lights. Loop detectors are placed in the road just beyond the stop line. Cameras are mounted in cabinets on hinged poles. Cables connect the loop detectors, the camera, and either the red light or the junction signal controller. If, more than a certain length of time after the light has turned to red, a vehicle crosses the stop line and activates the loop detectors, then a photograph of it is taken. Another photograph is taken a short while after, to show that the vehicle did not stop just beyond the stop line. Besides considering the technology, the paper also considers its effectiveness as a means of enforcement.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Recent developments in electronic systems for road tunnels and bridges
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: At a crossing (tunnel, bridge or combination thereof), there may be any type of traffic management requirement from none to a system of tidal flow and tolls. With the greater traffic loading of many crossings and their increased use in motorway networks, greater reliance is placed on the use of electronic systems, which help to increase traffic flow, reduce staffing costs and accidents and provide better records for maintenance and information for operation. Major systems currently in use include those for traffic control (on approaches and within the crossing), traffic surveillance (by CCTV inductive loops, etc.), plant monitoring and control, communications (by radio and telephone), and toll collection. This paper reviews the major developments of recent years, with reference to appropriate examples.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Assignment issues of route guidance systems
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Addresses four modelling issues, related to traffic assignment, that in the author's view deserve more attention before successful implementation of route guidance can be expected. The author concentrates on dynamic electronic route guidance systems, such as AUTOGUIDE and ALI-SCOUT, as opposed to systems that concentrate on map display. Most likely, the former will put higher requirements on the traffic model, and have a greater impact on congestion and travel times.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High traffic flows with low headway systems
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper puts the case for developing an automatic control system to augment the traffic capacity of motorways, and considers by means of a safety assessment of a particular system whether it may be practicable. The proposal uses lateral and low headway control systems for the right hand lanes of motorways. A vehicle would be driven under full manual control onto the right hand, low headway lane and would then be switched to automatic control. It would be guided along the lane at the speed at which the system is set. As it catches up with any vehicle its speed would be reduced so that it closely follows the vehicle just ahead. Other vehicles might then catch up with it and thus a 'train' of road vehicles would be formed. Any driver wishing to leave the train and the right hand lane would switch off automatic control and steer off the lane when a gap in the traffic opens up in the lane to its left.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Designing the charging protocol for 'Rekening Rijden'
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Rekening Rijden is a road charging system aimed at a reduction of traffic flow. The charging protocol defines the interchange of messages forming a passage charging transaction. The paper describes the protocol at its present stage of development and discusses some of the challenges that were to be met. Points of interest are: the solution of timing problems within the constraints imposed by smart cards; the division of the transaction area into zones; and a protocol for multilane situations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ramp metering control in the Netherlands
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Surveys conducted on the performance and effectiveness of the first metering scheme on motorway access ramps in the Netherlands showed improvements in traffic operations on the motorway. The number of 'rat runners' decreased dramatically, the travel time from the ramps along the A10 decreased, the speed in front of a tunnel increased, and there is no longer a delay for public transport travelling along the S101 ramp. Driver compliance with the ramp signals has been very good, with no more than 2 to 5% violations of the red 'stop' signal. No enforcement has been necessary.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The integration of road transport informatics for demand management
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Urban congestion is one of the most serious problems facing transportation experts today. As traffic levels grow, the economic and environmental effects of congestion are being increasingly felt, and effective solutions are therefore being sought in many cities around the world. One possible solution to the congestion problem lies in implementing demand management measures in order to limit demand for available roadspace. New and emerging technologies show significant potential for implementing and enforcing demand management measures, within an integrated system framework. The term 'road transport informatics' is currently used in Europe to describe a broad range of such technologies and systems, which can be used for various applications in the field of highway transportation. The paper describes current progress on a major European study into the use of road transport informatics in implementing demand management policies in urban areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Advanced integration of LRT and traffic signals
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The Los Angeles Light Rail Transit (LRT) system will open on 4 July 1990. It will interact in various ways with the heavy rail and road systems. After a general description of the system, the article discusses the need for active signal priority and the objectives which the signal system seeks to meet. The components of the system-detectors, travel time predictors and controllers, and the central computer and SCADA centre,-are described. The system's operation is then considered, and failure management is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Advances in traffic control systems in the United States to facilitate urban mobility
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Presents four areas covering some of the advances in traffic management systems which have been used in the United States in the battle against urban congestion. In the first two areas, integrated systems and ramp metering, the authors discuss exceptional practices using available technology which are being promoted for routine implementation throughout the country. The last areas, video imaging for wide area vehicle detection and in-vehicle motorist information, represent two applications of advanced technologies for use in traffic management systems. As development continues in these areas, and as technology advances, these applications may become more widely used, providing even greater opportunities for applying advanced traffic management techniques throughout urban areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Junction design and congested route choice
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Further traffic control systems are likely to involve strategies for congestion control, so that anticipated 'chaotic' conditions can be pre-empted by system responses which aim to achieve a more orderly pattern of 'queueing'. The maximum returns on investment are unlikely to be achieved by systems alone, without also upgrading geometric layouts at junctions. The paper considers the implications of this in general terms, and describes the traffic modelling methods being used to design junction improvements for the central road network in Leicester.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Variable speed advisory signals for linking coordinated systems in Canada
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: In the City of St. Albert, Alberta, Canada, variable speed advisory signals were installed in 1988 in order to improve the operation of a major roadway which connects the City of St. Albert with the City of Edmonton. These signals link two groups of signalized intersections operating under fixed time coordinated programs with different cycle times during most of the critical periods of the day. The influence of the speed advisory signals on traffic flow was evaluated in 1989. Delay and cyclic flow profile studies indicated that these signals had a positive effect on traffic flow. The paper describes the design and the operation of the speed advisory signal system and identifies the associated benefits and problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Group control of traffic at roundabouts
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper presents the application of the group traffic control methodology to signal controlled roundabouts. This methodology is based on the group model of traffic in street network. There are three types of elements in the model: groups of vehicles, road segments and control signals. Interactions among vehicle groups and the influence of signal or road on their movement are described by the set of seven elementary transformations. In this framework the optimal cycle time and offsets are derived for four-arm roundabout excluding the blocking back effect from circulating carriageway. The new method was proved to be very efficient in stops, delay and capacity on two roundabouts in Poznan.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Pelican crossing operation in areas under UTC
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Pedestrian crossings are installed to provide pedestrians with a safe method of crossing the road without incurring excessive delay. The paper considers the effect of urban traffic control (UTC) systems based on TRANSYT or SCOOT on the operation and utility of Pelican crossings and explores ways in which pedestrian delay could be reduced without imposing a significant disbenefit on vehicular traffic.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dilemma and option zones, the problem and countermeasures-characteristics of zones, and a new strategy of signal control for minimizing zones
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper presents the characteristics of dilemma zone and option zone, where a driver can either stop or legally pass through the intersection, revealed by the data analyses on vehicle behaviour and the existing serious problems on using the constant clearance intervals and, as a countermeasure, a new strategy of signal control for minimizing dilemma and option zones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fibre-optic axle sensors for vehicle data collection
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: Axle sensors are extensively used in traffic counting and classification systems. Most modern axle sensors are constructed of piezoelectric plastics. These give good all round performance and, coupled with charge amplifiers, offer reasonable sensitivity and low speed performance. Fibre-optic materials are now being investigated for two principal reasons. First, as piezoelectricity is generated by mechanical impulses, such sensors do not respond to static loads. Unfortunately, as congestion increases (and sites of traffic interest are often those where congestion occurs), stationary or very slowly moving vehicles are increasingly common. Fibre-optic sensors offer static as well as dynamic measurement. Secondly, a replaceable 'Tee' section piezoelectric sensor costs over Pounds 150, and fibre-optic technology, because of its wide use in the communications industry, has the potential to become the basis of cheaper sensors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Infrared detector development (road traffic sensors)
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Road Traffic Control, 1990.
abstract: The paper describes developments in the field of infrared road traffic sensors. It first discusses active and passive vehicle sensors. It then discusses pedestrian sensing systems and how they may be used to extend crossing time at a controlled crossing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
